supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.
supplier_interfaces.use: The local proper-prior convention follows this interface; the fixed-fiber formula separately admits sigma-finite improper priors.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.
supplier_interfaces.use: The local Definition treats measurability of each likelihood section as explicit data and makes no parameter-measurability inference.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.
supplier_interfaces.use: The prior Π is a measure; the local proposition proves that its likelihood-weighted integral is also a measure.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
supplier_interfaces.use: This supplies the meaning of the evidence and weighted-set integrals.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.
supplier_interfaces.use: This is the declared prior-measure class.

inspected_page_context.excerpt:
Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.
inspected_page_context.use: Terminological boundary: a posterior RCD is sample-point indexed; a data-indexed posterior is a probability kernel satisfying conditional identities, and null-data versions are not fixed. BCS-02 does not assert this for improper priors.

The proper-prior definition matches the local convention; the RCD definition supplies the sample-point/data-indexed distinction and null-version caveat. The two standard-Borel results are not imported by the BCS-02 dominated route. These drafts are not independently accepted.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim:
Define $
u_y(A):=\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$. By [F2], $
u_y$ is a measure and $
u_y(\Theta)=Z$ by the Statement's definition of $Z$ and the definition of the integral over a measurable set. Since $c$ is finite and positive, $c
u_y$ is also a measure and has total mass $cZ$, with the extended-real convention $c\cdot(+\infty)=+\infty$.

If $0<Z<+\infty$, then $c\nu_y$ is a probability exactly when $cZ=1$ by [F3], which is equivalent to $c=Z^{-1}$. If $Z=0$, its total mass is zero; if $Z=+\infty$, its total mass is infinite. Thus neither endpoint admits such a $c$, proving both directions without forming a quotient there.

prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

derivations.claim: The likelihood sections are normalized: $L_0(a)=1$, $L_1(b)=1$, and all other parameter-data pairs have likelihood zero. Therefore $Z(0)=1/2$, $Z(1)=1/2$, and $Z(2)=0$.

By [F3], the prior-predictive mass at $2$ is $Z(2)$ times its counting measure, hence zero. At this fiber every numerator $\int_A L_2\,d\Pi$ is also zero, so the displayed quotient is $0/0$ and is not defined; the theorem's chosen filler is $K(2,A)=\Pi(A)$. This filler is a version value on a prior-predictive null event, not an update inferred from the observation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F6], countable choice is available for [F3]. The boxes $E_k=(-k,k]$ have finite measure $2k$ and cover $\mathbb R$ by [F3], so $\lambda$ is sigma-finite. Since $E_k\subseteq\mathbb R$, [F4] gives $\lambda(\mathbb R)\ge2k$ for every $k$, hence $\lambda(\mathbb R)=+\infty$ and the flat prior is improper.

Fix $\mu$ and set $T(x)=(x-\mu)/\sigma$. This is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ with inverse $t\mapsto\mu+\sigma t$ and $|T'(x)|=1/\sigma$. The formula for $q_\mu$ is continuous in $x$, hence Borel by [F12] and Lebesgue measurable by [F15]. Since $\phi$ is also Lebesgue measurable by [F5, F15], [F7] gives $\int_{\mathbb R}q_\mu\,d\lambda=\int_{\mathbb R}\phi\,d\lambda=1$. The set function $P_\mu(A)=\int_Aq_\mu\,d\lambda$ is a measure by [F16], and its total mass one makes it a probability by [F17]. For a Borel $A$, apply [F7] to $f=\mathbf1_Aq_\mu$ and $S(z)=\mu+\sigma z$: $$N(\mu,\sigma^2)(A)=\int \mathbf1_A(S(z))\phi(z)\,d\lambda(z)=\int_A q_\mu(x)\,d\lambda(x),$$ since $\sigma q_\mu(S(z))=\phi(z)$ and [F14] defines $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ as this affine pushforward. Thus each coordinate law has the stated density.

Put $S=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2$. Expanding and using $\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)=0$ gives $\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2=S+n(\mu-\bar y)^2$. Hence $L_{\mathbf y}(\mu)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-S/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-n(\mu-\bar y)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. This is continuous in $\mu$, hence Borel by [F12] and $\mathcal L(\mathbb R)$-measurable by [F15]; therefore its evidence integral is defined by [F1].

For $k\ge1$, recursively form the finite product data measure $
u_k=\lambda^{\otimes k}$ on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R)^{\otimes k}$ using [F8] and [F9]. Starting from the sigma-finite $\lambda$, [F10] ensures that each $
u_k$ exists and is sigma-finite. The coordinate projections are measurable by [F8], so each pullback of $q_\mu$ is measurable by step 1.2; finite multiplication is continuous, making $f_k(y_1,\ldots,y_k)=\prod_{i=1}^kq_\mu(y_i)$ product-measurable. Step 1.2 gives $\int f_1\,d
u_1=1$. If $\int f_k\,d
u_k=1$, the recursive product definition and Tonelli [F11] give $\int f_{k+1}\,d
u_{k+1}=\int f_k\,d
u_k\int q_\mu\,d\lambda=1$. Thus $P_{\mu,n}(E):=\int_E f_n\,d
u_n$ is a measure by [F16] and a probability by [F17]. For measurable rectangles $E=A_1	imes\cdots	imes A_n$, repeated Tonelli gives $P_{\mu,n}(E)=\prod_{i=1}^nP_\mu(A_i)$. The product measure theorem [F10], iterated over the finite factors, identifies $P_{\mu,n}$ as the product of the one-coordinate laws. Therefore these coordinates are independent and $L_{\mathbf y}(\mu)$ is their joint density.

Set $T(\mu)=\sqrt n(\mu-\bar y)/\sigma$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ with inverse $u\mapsto\bar y+\sigma u/\sqrt n$ and derivative $\sqrt n/\sigma$. Since $e^{-u^2/2}=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\phi(u)$ is nonnegative and Lebesgue measurable by [F5, F15], [F7] gives $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-n(\mu-\bar y)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,d\lambda(\mu)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\sqrt{2\pi}$. Integrating the factorization in step 1.3 against the flat prior gives $Z(\mathbf y)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-S/(2\sigma^2)}\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt n}$, which is strictly positive and finite for every finite data vector.

Dividing step 1.3 by the finite positive evidence in step 2.2 gives $h(\mu)=\frac{\sqrt n}{\sigma}\phi\!\left(\frac{\sqrt n(\mu-\bar y)}{\sigma}\right)$, the displayed Lebesgue density. Put $s=\sigma/\sqrt n>0$; $S(z)=\bar y+sz$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\mu\mapsto(\mu-\bar y)/s$. For every Borel $A$, [F14] defines $N(\bar y,s^2)$ as this pushforward; [F7] applied to $f=\mathbf1_Ah$, which is Lebesgue measurable by [F12, F13, F15], gives $$\int_Ah(\mu)\,d\lambda(\mu)=\int\mathbf1_A(S(z))h(S(z))s\,d\lambda(z)=\int\mathbf1_A(S(z))\phi(z)\,d\lambda(z)=N(\bar y,s^2)(A).$$ The update on the full Lebesgue sigma-algebra is a probability by [F2]. If $n=0$ were allowed, its empty-product likelihood would be $1$ and the evidence would be $\lambda(\mathbb R)=+\infty$ by step 1.1, so no normalized update would exist.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F7], countable choice is available for [F3] and [F4]. Write $f(p)=1/[p(1-p)]$ on $(0,1)$. For any continuous $g:(0,1)\to\mathbb R$ and every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, continuity makes $g^{-1}(U)$ open in the subspace $(0,1)$, so $g^{-1}(U)=O\cap(0,1)$ for some open $O\subseteq\mathbb R$. Rational open intervals form a countable base, hence this intersection is a countable union of intervals with finite endpoints. Each is Lebesgue measurable by [F4], so $g^{-1}(U)$ belongs to the restricted Lebesgue sigma-algebra on $(0,1)$. Since open sets generate the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R$, $g$ is measurable for that restricted sigma-algebra. This applies to $f$ and to every binomial likelihood section, which is a polynomial. Thus [F5] defines the prior measure $\Pi(A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda$. For integers $k\ge3$, the sets $E_k=[1/k,1-1/k]$ cover $(0,1)$ and $f(p)\le k^2$ on $E_k$. Their Lebesgue lengths are at most one by [F4], so homogeneity and monotonicity [F6] give $\Pi(E_k)\le k^2<\infty$; [F3] makes this a sigma-finite prior. It is not finite: on each disjoint interval $I_j=(2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, $j\ge1$, one has $f(p)\ge1/p\ge2^j$ and $\lambda(I_j)=2^{-j-1}$ by [F4]. Homogeneity and monotonicity [F6] give $\Pi(I_j)=\int_{I_j}f\,d\lambda\ge1/2$. By [F5], $\Pi$ is a measure, so the prior mass of the union of the first $m$ such intervals is at least $m/2$ for every $m$. Hence $\Pi((0,1))=+\infty$ and the prior is improper.

For $y=0$, put $
u_0(A):=\int_A L_0\,d\Pi$; it is a measure by [F5], and $Z(0)=
u_0((0,1))$ by [F1]. The likelihood is $L_0(p)= inom n0(1-p)^n=(1-p)^n$, so on each $I_j$ from step 1.1, $p\le1/2$ gives $L_0(p)\ge2^{-n}$. Also $\Pi(I_j)\ge1/2$ by step 1.1. Monotonicity and homogeneity [F6] therefore give $
u_0(I_j)\ge2^{-n-1}$. The intervals are pairwise disjoint, so measure additivity gives $
u_0( igcup_{j=1}^m I_j)\ge m2^{-n-1}$; since this union is contained in $(0,1)$, countable additivity gives $
u_0((0,1))\ge m2^{-n-1}$ for every $m$. Thus $Z(0)=+\infty$ and [F1] leaves the quotient undefined.

For $y=n$, put $
u_n(A):=\int_A L_n\,d\Pi$; it is a measure by [F5], and $Z(n)=
u_n((0,1))$ by [F1]. Here $L_n(p)= inom nn p^n=p^n$. On each reflected interval $J_j=[1-2^{-j},1-2^{-j-1})$, $j\ge1$, one has $p\ge1/2$, so $L_n(p)\ge2^{-n}$. Also $f(p)\ge1/(1-p)\ge2^j$ there and $\lambda(J_j)=2^{-j-1}$ by [F4], so $\Pi(J_j)\ge1/2$ by [F6]. Monotonicity and homogeneity [F6] give $
u_n(J_j)\ge2^{-n-1}$. The intervals are pairwise disjoint, and additivity followed by nonnegativity on their complement gives $Z(n)=
u_n((0,1))\ge m2^{-n-1}$ for every $m$. Thus $Z(n)=+\infty$ and [F1] leaves this quotient undefined. By [F2], neither endpoint fiber admits a normalized posterior probability.
